newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan rivals fight fierce battle near Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rivals fight fierce battle near Kabul.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban movement and the opposition alliance exchanged artillery and rocket fire and bombed each other's positions near Kabul on Monday in some of the fiercest clashes of a two-week-old battle for the capital.

The opposition general controlling the front line at this already devastated village, about three km (two miles) from where the two sides were exchanging fire, said his so-called Northern Alliance forces killed at least 40 troops of the Islamic fundamentalist Taleban movement that holds the capital.
General Besmullah Khan told reporters his forces also destroyed one Taleban tank and captured another during the battle that lasted at least six hours at two key points on the capital's battlefront.
Taleban forces used helicopter gunships in their bid to break through the strategic villages of Zima and Hussainkot which mark the front line.
Russian jets on both sides dropped 500-lb bombs on each other's forces.
The Taleban bombing attack shortly after midday was directed against Khan's frontline headquarters.
A bomb landed only about 800 metres (yards) from where the general was directing his forces in the battle. There were no casualties at the headquarters.
About 50 refugees, carrying what they could on their backs and including about half a dozen young children, walked down the road away from the fighting towards territory controlled by the alliance.
Khan told Reuters it was the sixth time the Taleban forces had tried to punch their way through Zima and Hussainkot in a bid to relieve pressure on the capital.
"We have beaten them all again, but they keep trying," he said.
The opposition forces rushed about 100 reinforcements up to the front line and armoured personnel carriers rode up the highway carrying extra artillery ammunition.
Journalists at the headquarters saw more than a dozen large plumes of smoke rising into the air from rebel artillery and rocket fire.
Taleban forces replied in kind and, as well as the bombing attack near the headquarters, there was another bombing run about three km (two miles) into ground held by the alliance.
The crackle of small arms fire and heavy machine-gun fire was easily heard in the battle, which was carried out in scorching 47 degrees Celsius (116 F) temperature.
Despite all the fighting, by the time the battle died down in mid-afternoon, there appeared to be little change in either side's positions.
Two weeks ago, the opposition forces led by legendary guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood advanced to within 12 miles (20 km) of Kabul.
Since then there has been little significant change in the front line, but independent observers say that the opposition has been sending more men and supplies down to the battle zone.
The Taleban, who control two-thirds of Afghanistan, have vowed to take the whole country and rid it of warlords it blames for chaos since the defeat of the communist regime five years ago.
